newsitem.title: DUBAI: Americans in Saudi warned against fresh attacks.
newsitem.headline: Americans in Saudi warned against fresh attacks.

text.p: The U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday warned Americans in the kingdom to raise their guard against further attacks following fresh threats by a leading Islamist dissident.
"Planning for terrorist action against U.S. interests in Saudi Arabia continues unabated," callers to a security hotline were told in a recorded message.

Security alerts have been a frequent feature of daily life for the 35,000-strong American community in Saudi Arabia since five U.S. military advisers and two Indians were killed by a car bomb in the capital Riyadh 15 months ago.
A second bomb last June in the eastern city of Khobar killed 19 U.S. airmen and injured hundreds of others. Four Saudis were beheaded for the first bombing. The second remains under investigation.

Callers to the hotline at the U.S. embassy in Riyadh and the U.S. consulates in Dhahran and Jeddah were told that the embassy noted with deep concern an interview on British television last Thursday "with well-known terrorist Osama bin Laden in which he not only threatened again the U.S. military in Saudi Arabia but also called for the expulsion of American civilians".

Bin Laden, who led Arab fighters in the war against Soviet troops in Afghanistan in the 1980s, is a Saudi-born financier who has been stripped of his citizenship and has threatened to wage holy war against Americans in the birthplace of Islam.
U.S. officials have named him as a prime suspect in the two bombings and "one of the most significant sponsors of Islamic extremist activities in the world today".

The latest U.S. security warning said "the embassy continues to receive reports indicating possible surveillance or probes of U.S. military and government facilities suggesting that planning for terrorist action against U.S. interests in Saudi Arabia continues unabated".

It said the period after the recent Moslem festival of Eid al-Fitr was considered particularly dangerous in light of a public threat that attacks would occur if certain detained individuals were not released before the end of the holy fasting month of Ramadan, which ended on February 8.

The upcoming month of pilgrimage, due to start in mid-April, raised further concerns because the large inflow of pilgrims placed a heavy burden on the entire Saudi government, but most particularly the security forces, the embassy added.
"These statements and reports reinforce the embassy's view of the need for the private American community in Saudi Arabia to heighten its vigilance and alertness," it said.
About two million Moslems -- half of them from abroad -- visit the holy city of Mecca during the annual haj pilgrimage, one of the five pillars of Islam.
One security concern in recent years has been attempts by Iranian pilgrims to hold rallies against the United States and Israel during haj.
In 1987 Saudi security forces in Mecca clashed with demonstrators in one such rally, killing about 400 people, mainly Iranians.
Iran on Monday vowed its pilgrims would defy a Saudi ban and hold the political rally denouncing the United States and Israel as enemies of Islam.

The latest U.S. warning came as a high-level Saudi Arabian delegation led by Prince Sultan, deputy prime minister and Minister of Aviation and Defence, was visiting Washington to allay Clinton administration concerns over the probe into last year's bombing.
The close U.S.-Saudi relationship has been dogged in recent months by Washington's complaints that Riyadh was not sharing enough information on its investigation into the June blast.
